paragraphs.heading: What a rock is
paragraphs.text: In geology, the word rock, or stone, covers any solid mass, or aggregate, of minerals or of mineraloid matter that occurs naturally. A rock is categorized by the minerals in it, by its chemical composition and by the way it formed. Rocks make up the crust, which is the Earth's outer solid layer, and most of its interior. The exceptions are the outer core, which is liquid, and pockets of magma in the asthenosphere.

paragraphs.heading: What rocks are made of
paragraphs.text: Rocks are made mainly of grains of minerals. A mineral is a crystalline solid, formed from atoms that are chemically bonded into an orderly structure. Some rocks also hold mineraloids. These are rigid substances that resemble minerals but lack crystalline structure; volcanic glass is one. Most rocks contain silicate minerals, compounds with silica tetrahedra in their crystal lattice. Silicate minerals account for roughly a third of all known mineral species, and for about 95% of the Earth's crust.

paragraphs.heading: Three main groups
paragraphs.text: Rocks are usually sorted into three main groups: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Igneous rocks form when magma cools inside the Earth's crust, or when lava cools on the seabed or the ground surface. Sedimentary rocks form from sediments, by processes called diagenesis and lithification. The sediments themselves come from the weathering, transport and deposition of existing rocks. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are put under pressures and temperatures so high that they are transformed without significant melting.

paragraphs.heading: No sharp lines between them
paragraphs.text: Given time, one type of rock can be transformed into another. A geological model called the rock cycle describes this. The three classes are subdivided into many groups, but there are no hard-and-fast boundaries between allied rocks. As the proportions of their minerals rise or fall, rocks pass by gradations from one kind into the next. Rock names therefore just correspond to selected points in a continuously graded series.

paragraphs.heading: A closer look at igneous rock
paragraphs.text: Igneous rock takes its name from the Latin ignis, meaning fire, and forms when magma or lava cools and solidifies. When magma cools and crystallizes slowly inside the Earth's crust, the result is plutonic, or intrusive, rock; granite is a common example. When magma reaches the surface, as lava or as fragmental ejecta, the result is volcanic, or extrusive, rock. Magmas tend to grow richer in silica as they rise towards the surface, a process called magma differentiation. By volume, about 65% of the Earth's crust is igneous rock.

paragraphs.heading: Rocks and people
paragraphs.text: People have used rocks since the time of the earliest humans. That early period is called the Stone Age, and it saw many stone tools developed. Stone then went into buildings and early infrastructure as a major component of their construction. Mining grew up as a way to take rocks out of the Earth and obtain the minerals in them, metals included. Modern technology has made it possible to develop new rocks made by humans, along with rock-like substances such as concrete.

paragraphs.heading: How rocks are studied
paragraphs.text: Petrology studies the character and origin of rocks, and mineralogy studies the mineral components that create them. The study of rocks became a formal science during the 19th century. Radioactive decay was discovered in 1896, which allowed rocks to be dated by radiometric dating. Plate tectonics came to be understood in the 20th century's second half.
